headline: Oil shrugged off a Russia Ukraine 'energy ceasefire' that fell apart within hours and is back near $106, while a 3.65% drop in Korea's KOSPI drags memory chips lower before banks, CPI and TSMC.
summary: US stock futures are flat this Columbus Day morning: S&P 500 futures were up about 0.1% near 7,865 and the bond market is closed. Trump announced a Russia Ukraine 'energy ceasefire' over the weekend, crude fell more than 1% overnight, then Zelensky said Russia ignored it within hours and Brent climbed back above $106 as Iran said Hormuz stays shut until its terms are met. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 from $85, a sign that even bears are moving up. In Asia, Korea's KOSPI fell 3.65% to 6,384 as foreigners sold Samsung and SK Hynix for a tenth straight session, and Micron was down about 2% premarket after China's CXMT moved a new memory platform into mass production. Medtronic's MiniMed swap was heavily oversubscribed, so it will retire the maximum 55 million shares. No setup can trigger before today's close, so the plan is to watch which names hold up on real volume into Tuesday's bank and health earnings.

regime.why: Oil keeps finding buyers above $100 even on peace headlines, so the inflation risk into Wednesday's CPI has not gone away. Stocks are near records, but memory chips and Korea are cracking on foreign selling tied to rising US borrowing costs. Normal size only on breakouts that confirm on volume; stay small in rate sensitive and travel names.

signals.title: Trump's Russia Ukraine 'energy ceasefire' knocked oil down for a few hours, then crude went back up
signals.what_happened: Over the weekend Trump said Russia and Ukraine agreed to stop hitting each other's energy sites, effective at once. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed it, and Zelensky said Russia ignored it within hours. Trump made a similar claim in mid September that was also never confirmed. Brent for December first fell about 0.2% to $104.54 and WTI 0.4% to $91.48 (Investing.com), and CNBC saw both down more than 1% overnight. By Monday morning WTI was up 1.2% at $93.00 and Brent was above $106, with Iran saying Hormuz stays shut until its conditions are met (ZeroHedge). Diesel and heating oil held most of their drop. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 from $85, citing the risk of new escalation.
signals.so_what: Two separate wars feed oil prices. A real stop to strikes on Russian refineries would ease diesel, which is why heating oil stayed lower. But crude is set by Hormuz, and nothing changed there. Second order: refiners and diesel users (truckers, airlines) get a small break only if the truce holds, while crude producers keep their edge. Third order: oil that holds above $100 into Wednesday's CPI keeps rate hike talk alive, which is the main risk to richly priced tech. What would make this wrong: Russia confirms the truce and Iran accepts the US Hormuz proposal in the same week.
signals.for_you: Swing: XOM (entry 170.64, needs 20.6M+ shares) and CVX (entry 218.23, needs 12.9M+ shares) get the oil tailwind, but a gap on light volume is still a wait. Puts: oil names carry richer premium on days like this; see Setups for live quotes and do not sell into a spike in the first hour. Long term: no action; peace headlines that Russia does not confirm are not a reason to sell energy.

signals.title: Gulf follow up: a second Riyadh airport attack, Iran calls the US Hormuz offer 'insufficient', Gulf stocks slip
signals.since_yesterday: Saudi authorities said Sunday's new attack on Riyadh airport killed one more person and wounded 11 (CNN), the Saturday toll rose to at least 13, and Iran called the latest US proposal to reopen Hormuz 'insufficient'.
signals.what_happened: The Houthis claimed another strike on King Khalid airport on Sunday Oct 11. CNN reports it killed a Pakistani resident and wounded 11, and that an Indian man hurt on Saturday later died, so Saturday's toll is at least 13. Iran called the newest US plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz 'insufficient', and attacks on tankers there have continued this month (Investing.com). Saudi Arabia's TASI fell 0.15% to 10,360.74 on Sunday after bigger early losses, Saudi National Bank fell about 1.1%, and Qatar's index fell about 1.5%. A newsletter said a drone hit a tanker anchorage near Hormuz on Monday, but no news outlet confirmed it.
signals.so_what: Saudi Arabia is now under steady attack at home, not just at sea, so the Gulf bypass routes it built around Hormuz are also at risk. That keeps a war premium in oil and in shipping insurance. Iran rejecting the US offer means the Feb 28 closure goes on, so Qatar LNG stays stuck and US LNG stays in demand. No new word on whether the US will join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
signals.for_you: Swing: no new trades on the headline alone; let XOM and CVX prove it with breakout volume. Puts: if you sell puts on energy, pick strikes under support you would own through a sudden peace deal, which could drop oil fast. Long term: LNG (US LNG exporter) stays a beneficiary of stuck Qatar cargoes; it is not on the Lineup, so do your own valuation first.

signals.title: Memory chips crack: KOSPI falls 3.65% as foreigners dump Samsung and SK Hynix, Micron lower premarket
signals.what_happened: Korea's KOSPI fell 3.65% to 6,384.24 on Oct 12, its lowest close since Aug 11 (Aju Press). Samsung closed down 4.39% at 250,500 won and SK Hynix down 4.52% at 1.605 million won (TradingKey). Foreigners sold a net 2.02 trillion won (about $1.51 billion), a tenth straight day of selling, and local brokers tied it to rising US borrowing costs. In US premarket trade Micron fell about 2%, SanDisk about 2%, and Western Digital and Seagate more than 1%, after China's CXMT said its fifth generation DRAM platform (G5) is in mass production; CXMT's share of world DRAM was about 10% in Q2 2026 per Counterpoint. Optical names went the other way premarket: Lumentum up about 5% and Coherent up about 3.4%. TSMC rose about 1% before Thursday's results.
signals.so_what: Memory makers ran up because AI servers created a shortage; the risk was always that China adds supply and prices roll over. Most of Micron's recent sales growth came from higher prices, not more chips, so it is exposed if CXMT keeps adding output. Second order: the money leaving memory is not leaving AI. It is rotating to optics and TSMC, where capacity is sold out (Lumentum said Oct 9 its optical capacity is committed into early 2029). Third order: Korea is a foreign money barometer. Ten straight days of selling while Samsung guides to record profit says global funds are cutting risk as US rates rise. What would make this wrong: TSMC on Thursday raises 2027 capex and says memory supply stays tight.
signals.for_you: Swing: ANET (entry 217.85, needs 8.9M+ shares) is AI networking, not memory, but a chip selloff can drag it; wait for the volume. Avoid new swings in MU, SNDK, WDC and STX into a falling tape. Puts: memory names have high premium now, but do not sell puts on a stock that is breaking down. Long term: COHR is in the Buy zone and LITE is Accumulate on pullback on the dashboard; a broad chip selloff is the kind of dip that puts LITE back near its buy zone.

signals.title: Medtronic's MiniMed swap was oversubscribed: it will retire the maximum 55 million shares
signals.since_yesterday: Preliminary results Oct 12: only about 18.3% of tendered shares will be taken, and Medtronic will accept 55,032,401 of its shares for all 252,813,348 MiniMed shares it was offering.
signals.what_happened: Medtronic said its exchange offer was oversubscribed. It plans to accept 55,032,401 Medtronic shares, the top of the range, in exchange for 252,813,348 MiniMed shares at the 4.5939 ratio. The preliminary proration factor is about 18.3%, which implies roughly 300 million Medtronic shares were tendered. Holders of fewer than 100 shares who tendered everything are not prorated. The final factor comes Oct 14.
signals.so_what: Medtronic shrinks its share count by about 55 million without spending cash, which lifts earnings per share and leaves it free of the diabetes business. The heavy demand shows holders wanted the discount to MiniMed. The other side: about 253 million MiniMed shares now sit with new holders who got them at a discount, and many will sell. MiniMed's float jumps, which can weigh on the stock for weeks.
signals.for_you: Long term: MDT is in the Buy zone on the dashboard and gets a cleaner, smaller share base; a reasonable name to buy in tranches or sell puts on at a strike you would own. Swing: avoid MMED while new holders sell. No action needed until the Oct 14 final count.

signals.title: Self driving gets two green lights: Waymo's first $5 billion loan and a five year federal pass for driverless trucks
signals.what_happened: Waymo closed a $5 billion term loan, its first ever debt, led by Pimco, Blackstone and Sixth Street with Goldman Sachs as bookrunner. It was upsized from about $3 billion and priced at 5.25 points over the benchmark rate; Waymo raised $16 billion of equity at a $126 billion value in February. Separately, the FMCSA granted a five year exemption, effective Oct 7, 2026 through Oct 7, 2031 and published Oct 9, that lets Level 4 driverless trucks use cab mounted warning beacons instead of putting out warning triangles. It replaces short waivers Aurora had run on since October 2025, and other carriers can opt in.
signals.so_what: Lenders like Pimco and Blackstone only lend against a business they think will generate cash, so the loan says robotaxis are moving from science project to fleet business. The money buys cars, sensors and compute, which flows to NVIDIA and lidar and car suppliers. For trucks, the warning triangle rule was the last everyday task that needed a human on board; with it gone, driverless freight can scale on the Texas lanes Aurora already runs. Who pays: human driven ride hail and trucking face a cheaper competitor over years, not months. What would make this wrong: a serious crash that brings back the rule or slows city permits.
signals.for_you: Long term: GOOGL (Waymo's parent) and AUR gain; this is a years long story, not a swing. Swing: no setup; AUR is volatile and not on the swing list. Puts: no action. Watch whether UBER and LYFT keep partnering with Waymo or start losing riders to it.

cycle.quadrant_why: September CPI due Wednesday is expected at about 3.6% to 3.7% a year, up from 3.4%, and Brent is back near $106 even after a peace headline. Growth is still positive: S&P 500 futures sit near 7,865, close to the record. In Dalio's four season view this is still the rising inflation season.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late. The Fed lifted rates to 3.75% to 4.00% on Sep 16 and the 10-year was 5.24% on Friday. Today's tell is abroad: Korean brokers blame ten days of foreign selling on rising US borrowing costs. In Dalio's model, late cycle tightening first shows up where foreign money is most mobile.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Public debt is high and long rates are above 5%. Even Waymo, backed by Alphabet, is paying 5.25 points over the base rate for its first loan, a reminder that money is no longer cheap for anyone.
cycle.big_cycle: Four of Dalio's five forces are active. Debt and money: high rates and high debt. Internal order: a split US three weeks before the Nov 3 midterms. External order: a Gulf war that now reaches Riyadh, a Russia Ukraine war with a truce no one confirmed, and US China rivalry in memory chips. Technology: the AI build out, still the main tailwind.
tailwinds: AI spending keeps flowing, now rotating toward optics and foundry (LITE, COHR, TSM) rather than memory.
Oil producers outside the Gulf earn more while Hormuz stays shut.
Big private lenders are funding real economy AI uses like robotaxis.
headwinds: Oil near $106 into CPI keeps rate hike odds alive.
Foreign money is leaving crowded chip markets like Korea.
China adding memory supply threatens the price gains that drove chip profits.

history.what: Oil quadrupled and inflation surged. The S&P 500 fell about 48% from its January 1973 high to the October 1974 low, and even Exxon and Chevron fell about 44%.
history.lesson: In a true oil shock with rising inflation, almost nothing is safe. Cash and short duration held up best.

source.title: Museum of American Finance: 1970s Bear Market

history.what: Oil nearly doubled from Aug 2 to Oct 11, 1990, and the S&P 500 fell about 17% over the same window. When the air campaign began in January 1991, stocks rose almost 20% in about a month.
history.lesson: War scares hit fast, but markets bottom when the uncertainty peaks, often before the news gets better.

source.title: TrendSpider: The Gulf War recession 1990 to 1991

history.what: The S&P 500 lost about 19% for the year and entered a bear market in June, while the energy sector returned more than 60%, the best sector by far.
history.lesson: In the rising inflation season, energy and real assets lead and long duration growth lags.

source.title: Investing Daily: The Leaders and Laggards of 2022

cycle.differences: The setup has not changed since Sunday, so the history stays. What is new is that peace headlines no longer move oil for long: this morning's truce was priced out within hours. Unlike 1973, the US is a big producer and the AI boom is a real growth engine; unlike 1990, there are two wars feeding energy prices, not one.
cycle.for_you: Swing: favor setups that confirm on volume in energy and AI infrastructure with real earnings; skip memory chips while they break down. Puts: sell only where you would own the stock through a 20% drop, and wait for Tuesday's earnings before selling puts on banks and health insurers. Long term: keep buying quality in tranches and keep cash for the kind of drawdown 1990 and 2022 brought.

principle.text: Don't confuse what you wish were true with what is really true.
principle.applied: Everyone wants a ceasefire, and the market bought the headline for a few hours. But Russia never confirmed it and Iran still has Hormuz shut, so crude went right back up. Trade on what the parties actually do, not on the announcement.
